Some readers of Schmeh's original 2014 German post noted possible transcription errors in hard-to-read letters (per this post's own text), so treat this as a secondary transcription pending an independent re-check against the image (rule 2).
alphabet: Latin letters, digits (5, 6, 19, 55, 519 etc.), and periods used throughout as separators between short tokens -- reads as an abbreviation-heavy text (periods after nearly every token, like a chancery-abbreviated Latin/German document) rather than a letter-substitution cryptogram in the usual sense

constraints.legend: per a popular local legend (Lazarus's own chronicle, per Schmeh, relaying reader Gert Brantner's tip), Lazarus found this text engraved in a rock inside a cave of the Untersberg massif (Salzburg/Berchtesgaden border region) and recorded it in his manuscript alongside 20 other illustrations
constraints.related_artifact: a metal plate bearing a very similar inscription is mentioned (linked image, not fetched, copyright-restricted per Schmeh) -- provenance of that plate is unknown to Schmeh
constraints.no_expert_examination: Schmeh, as of the post date: 'As far as I know, there is no examination of the Untersberg code made by an encryption expert'
constraints.form_hypothesis: Schmeh's own assessment: '16th century encryption systems were not especially secure... Some knowledge of ancient German or Latin might be more helpful than codebreaking skills'; he also flags the alternative that this is not an encryption at all but 'an abbreviated text, a meaningless letter sequence, or something else' -- the heavy periods-after-tokens pattern (constraints.alphabet) is exactly what a real 16th-century Latin/German abbreviation convention (not a cipher) looks like, and should be tested against that reading before assuming substitution
constraints.second_source: a reader (comment #1, 'Katrin') points to a higher-quality image reproduction at archivmedes.blogspot.de/2015/08/der-untersberg-code.html, sourced from the Salzburg Museum -- not fetched this pass (out of the seven named hosts for this brief)

cheap_tests_in_order: 1. Test the abbreviation hypothesis first, cheaply and without cryptanalysis: compare the token-and-period pattern (short Latin/German-looking fragments each closed with a period, occasional digits) against known 16th-century German/Latin scribal abbreviation conventions (e.g. standard Tironian-note-derived and suspension abbreviations) rather than assuming a substitution cipher -- Schmeh's own text already leans this way ('some knowledge of ancient German or Latin might be more helpful than codebreaking skills'). Cost $1, Sonnet.

2. Fetch Untersberg-Code.png (scienceblogs.de) and the higher-quality archivmedes.blogspot.de reproduction (a different host, not yet used this pass, still subject to the good-citizen one-request-at-a-time rule) to independently re-transcribe the six lines and check for the hard-to-read-letter errors the source itself flags; this is a precondition for trusting any downstream test, per rule 2. Cost $2.

3. If the abbreviation hypothesis (test 1) is rejected, run a monoalphabetic/homophonic substitution anneal against German and Latin separately (both plausible for a 16th-century Salzburg-region text), judged with matched controls at the same N and K, same solver. Cost $2-3.
matched_control: not yet run; test 3 above specifies the design if needed (synthetic German and Latin plaintext, same N/K, same solver) -- but test 1 (abbreviation hypothesis) should run first since a scribal-abbreviation reading would make a substitution-cipher control comparison the wrong test entirely (CLAUDE.md rule 3: match the design)

cheap_test_done.method: abbreviation-hypothesis pattern count (1-3 letters + period) vs synthetic control drawn i.i.d. from the target's own unigram character distribution, same length, 500 trials, seed 20260925 -- specs/cheap-tests/untersberg-code/test1_abbreviation.py
cheap_test_done.verdict: target ABOVE control range -- short-token/period clustering exceeds chance; supports the abbreviation-shaped reading over 'meaningless periods' but does not itself distinguish a real 16th-c. abbreviation convention from another structured design (no abbreviation-convention corpus on hand to test against directly). Not a reading, not closed-negative: control-backed positive signal only. See specs/cheap-tests/untersberg-code/README.md.
cheap_test_done.cost_usd_estimate: well under $1, disk-only, no hosts beyond intake
